case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may, consistent with the First Amendment, discipline a licensed counselor for engaging in talk therapy with a client—i.e., speech in a professional-client setting—when that speech is deemed to constitute prohibited “conversion therapy.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause); Colorado’s prohibition on licensed mental-health professionals engaging in “conversion therapy” (commonly enacted as a regulation of professional practice/discipline that bars certain counseling communications aimed at changing sexual orientation or gender identity).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner (a licensed counselor) argues that the Colorado law is a content- and viewpoint-based restriction on speech because it targets what counselors may say in therapy sessions based on the message (and often the direction) of the counseling. She contends that talk therapy is core speech, not merely conduct, and that the State cannot re-label disfavored counseling viewpoints as “professional conduct” to evade heightened First Amendment scrutiny. Petitioner and supporting amici emphasize that the law censors certain conversations and therapeutic goals, chills counselors’ and clients’ ability to discuss sensitive matters, and forces conformity with the State’s preferred orthodoxy on sexuality/gender-related counseling. They urge the Court to apply at least strict scrutiny (or, at minimum, heightened scrutiny) and to reject a broad ‘professional speech’ carve-out that would allow states to suppress disfavored ideas in the counseling room.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Colorado officials) maintain that the law is a permissible regulation of professional practice designed to protect patients from harmful or ineffective treatment, and that any impact on speech is incidental to regulating conduct within a licensed profession. They characterize the prohibited activity as a form of treatment modality (professional conduct) rather than protected expression, argue that states have longstanding authority to set standards of care and prohibit dangerous practices, and contend that the restriction is justified by substantial governmental interests in public health and patient safety. Respondents and supporting amici also argue that the law does not forbid discussion of sexuality or gender identity generally, but rather bars a specific practice the State deems harmful—so it should be reviewed under a more deferential standard than strict scrutiny (e.g., as regulation of professional conduct).
key_precedents: National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (2018)
Pickup v. Brown (9th Cir. 2014) (often cited in conversion-therapy litigation, though later circuit authority varies)
King v. Governor of New Jersey (3d Cir. 2014) (conversion-therapy context; later doctrinal tension after NIFLA)
Rumsfeld v. Forum for Academic & Institutional Rights, Inc. (FAIR) (2006)
Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey (1992) (frequently invoked in compelled/regulated medical speech debates)
Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel (1985) (government-mandated disclosures in professional/commercial speech)
Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project (2010) (speech coordinated with regulated conduct; often invoked in speech/conduct boundary arguments)
Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969) (general First Amendment baseline; cited in some speech-restriction frameworks)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett make the case’s hardest point: States possess broad authority to regulate licensed professional practice and to enforce standards of care even when doing so requires examining what was said. But here the State’s line is drawn on the communicative content and direction of the counselor’s words in a talk-therapy session, so the burden on speech is not merely incidental; it is the mechanism of regulation, as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, and NIFLA forecloses treating that as a lesser-protected ‘professional speech’ category. Once we recognize that the law operates in a content- and practical viewpoint-based manner, Colorado must justify this specific censorship of a consensual counseling conversation with a narrowly framed showing of harm from the particular exemption, not a broadly formulated appeal to public health. A narrower holding—limited to talk therapy consisting of speech and to viewpoint-discriminatory bans as applied—best addresses the State’s conduct-regulation concern while respecting the First Amendment’s threshold command against abridging speech.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett most forcefully argue that Colorado is regulating professional conduct—setting a standard of care for licensed counseling—and that any effect on speech is merely incidental. But that description fails Reed’s commonsense inquiry: the trigger for discipline is the content and direction of the counselor’s words in a talk-therapy session, which makes this a content- (and in operation, viewpoint-) based restriction on speech, not a regulation of nonexpressive conduct with collateral speech effects. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, NIFLA forecloses a freestanding “professional speech” carve-out that would let the State censor disfavored messages simply because they are delivered by a licensed professional. Colorado therefore must satisfy strict scrutiny, and on this record it has not shown a narrowly tailored justification for a categorical ban on one side of a consensual therapeutic conversation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett are right to emphasize the State’s latitude to regulate professional conduct and standards of care, even when enforcement requires reviewing what was said. But that framing does not fit this statute’s operative trigger: as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, Colorado disciplines counselors based on the communicative content and direction of their talk-therapy—permitting counseling that affirms certain outcomes while forbidding counseling aimed at others—making the law content- and viewpoint-based in operation. Under NIFLA, the State cannot evade heightened scrutiny by relabeling disfavored speech as “professional conduct,” and the categorical ban is not narrowly tailored on this record given obvious less speech-restrictive alternatives. Accordingly, I remain with Petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that because the prohibited “treatment” consists of words, the law necessarily targets speech by content and direction, triggering NIFLA and heightened scrutiny. But that elides the threshold question I think should control: Colorado is regulating a licensed professional practice for minors—setting a standard of care—and our cases have long allowed generally applicable conduct regulation even when enforcing it requires examining what was said and even when the practice is communicative. NIFLA rejected a free-floating “professional speech” category; it did not hold that every speech-infused regulation of professional treatment becomes a Reed-style censorship case, especially where the State is not compelling affirmation of its preferred message but proscribing a modality it deems harmful. Justice Barrett’s framing best fits the doctrinal limiting principle: without it, the First Amendment becomes a vehicle for broad exemptions from ordinary professional discipline whenever a regulated practice is carried out through dialogue.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (joined by Justice Barrett) is right to stress the State’s traditional authority to regulate professional conduct and enforce standards of care, even when doing so requires examining what was said. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch underscore, the prohibited “treatment” here is the communicative exchange itself—talk therapy—so liability turns on the content and direction of a counselor’s speech, not on some separable, nonexpressive procedure with merely incidental speech effects. NIFLA cautions against converting that fact into a de facto “professional speech” discount, and once strict scrutiny is triggered Colorado must show (Ashcroft-style) that less speech-restrictive tools—like informed consent, targeted prohibitions on coercion or fraud, or case-by-case discipline for demonstrable harm—would be equally ineffective, which it has not done on this record. Because this law does not fit within any historic and traditional unprotected category and its bluntness predictably chills protected dialogue in the counseling room, I remain with Petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett press the best objection: that Colorado is regulating professional conduct—a treatment modality for minors—and that any speech burden is incidental to a licensure-based standard of care. But on this record, the prohibited “treatment” is the counselor’s words themselves in a private talk-therapy session, and liability turns on the content and direction of that communication, not on the use of any nonexpressive procedure; that brings the case within NIFLA’s warning against downgrading speech by relabeling it “professional.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute’s asymmetry—permitting counseling that affirms certain outcomes while forbidding counseling aimed at different outcomes—looks like viewpoint-based censorship, and the threatened licensing penalties and compliance burdens supply the coercion that compelled-speech doctrine has long treated as constitutionally salient. Colorado may regulate fraud, coercion, malpractice, and genuinely nonexpressive conduct, but it has not shown a sufficiently tight fit to justify suppressing one side of a contested therapeutic conversation merely because it occurs in the counseling room.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett make the best point that States may regulate professional conduct and enforce standards of care even when speech is involved. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, this statute’s trigger for discipline is the communicative content and therapeutic direction of what the counselor says in talk therapy—the “treatment” is speech itself—so it functions as a content-based restriction and, in practical operation, a viewpoint-based one. NIFLA cautions that we cannot dilute First Amendment scrutiny by relabeling speech as “professional conduct,” and Colorado has not shown the kind of narrow tailoring required for a categorical ban where less speech-restrictive tools (informed consent, case-specific discipline for coercion or demonstrable harm) are available. Upholding this would invite States to police disfavored messages within licensed relationships by calling them “treatment,” which is not a historically rooted exception to ordinary First Amendment protection.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that this law is triggered by what is said in the room, so Reed/NIFLA content-discrimination analysis should control. But NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” doctrine; it did not strip States of their traditional authority to define and enforce standards of care for licensed providers treating minors, even when the treatment modality is communicative and enforcement necessarily examines the content of what was said. Recasting that professional-discipline setting as ordinary public “speech as speech” risks constitutionalizing a heightened First Amendment floor (strict scrutiny for any talk-based therapy regulation) untethered to history or our precedents about professional regulation, and it would give this context more protection than other routinely regulated, speech-infused professional practices. Colorado may be unwise to adopt a categorical ban, but I do not see a basis to treat this as viewpoint censorship rather than regulation of a specific licensed practice with only incidental burdens on speech, so I would uphold.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett press the serious point that States may set standards of care for licensed professionals and that enforcement will often require examining what was said. But that framing collapses the mechanism of the burden: here the regulated “treatment” is the counselor’s speech itself—talk therapy—and discipline turns on the content and directional thrust of the counselor’s words, making this unlike a nonexpressive procedure with only incidental speech effects (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, consistent with NIFLA’s rejection of a freestanding ‘professional speech’ carve-out). Once we identify the correct First Amendment framework for this factual mechanism, heightened scrutiny is triggered, and Colorado has not shown a sufficiently tailored fit for a categorical ban that predictably chills protected counselor-client dialogue. I would therefore stay with Petitioner, while keeping the holding tightly tethered to viewpoint-discriminatory bans on speech-based therapy rather than ordinary malpractice regulation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado’s law imposes a concrete burden on protected speech because it disciplines a counselor for what she says in a talk-therapy session, and on the counselor’s and client’s own understanding the prohibited act is communicative counseling directed toward certain goals and viewpoints. The restriction is content- and viewpoint-based: it turns on the subject (sexual orientation/gender identity change efforts) and the direction of the message (permitting counseling that affirms but forbidding counseling that seeks change), and the State cannot avoid First Amendment scrutiny by re-labeling disfavored counseling conversations as “professional conduct.” Under heightened review, Colorado must do more than invoke public health in the abstract; it must identify the specific harm of allowing this counselor to engage in consensual talk therapy with this client, and show that prohibiting that speech is narrowly tailored rather than a blunt ban on one side of a contested debate. On this record, the State’s broadly formulated interests do not justify categorical censorship in the counseling room where the regulation operates directly on speech.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado’s ban, as applied to a licensed counselor’s talk therapy, is content based under Reed’s commonsense inquiry because discipline turns on what is said in the counseling session—communications aimed at changing or reducing same-sex attraction or gender-related feelings—and thus it is presumptively invalid and triggers strict scrutiny. The State cannot avoid that result by relabeling pure speech as “professional conduct,” particularly after NIFLA rejected a free-standing “professional speech” category subject to lesser protection. Unlike regulations that target nonexpressive conduct with only incidental effects on expression (where O’Brien might apply), this law directly targets the communicative content and therapeutic viewpoint of the counselor’s speech in the counseling room. On this record, Colorado has not carried its burden to satisfy strict scrutiny, so disciplining the counselor violates the First Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado’s discipline is attributable to the State through its licensing and enforcement apparatus, and the First Amendment’s “no law” command—incorporated against the States—therefore applies in full to this professional-client setting. The statute targets speech as speech: it prohibits a counselor’s talk therapy based on the content and viewpoint of what is said (permitting counseling that affirms certain conclusions about sexual orientation or gender identity while forbidding counseling that pursues the opposite goal), and the State may not evade heightened scrutiny by relabeling disfavored viewpoints as “professional conduct.” NIFLA rejected a broad “professional speech” carve-out and warned that a licensing regime cannot be used to diminish First Amendment protection; here the law functions as viewpoint discrimination in a setting where private speakers otherwise may speak freely, and Colorado has not shown a sufficiently tailored justification to suppress one side of this debate. Because the regulation is content- and viewpoint-based censorship of private counseling speech rather than genuine government speech or a neutral standard of care, it triggers strict scrutiny and cannot stand on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado’s rule is best understood as a generally applicable regulation of professional practice—i.e., the permissible setting of a standard of care for licensed counselors treating clients—rather than a law dictating public debate or compelling a counselor to endorse the State’s preferred ideology. Although the prohibited treatment is delivered through words, the First Amendment has long permitted regulation of professional conduct that only incidentally burdens speech, and the State is disciplining the use of a specific therapeutic modality it deems harmful, not banning discussion of sexual orientation or gender identity writ large. The law does not compel the counselor to say anything to a client; it sets neutral conditions on the provision of licensed services, much like other professional-discipline regimes that turn on what a professional does in the course of treatment. Requiring some examination of what was said in session to determine whether the prohibited practice occurred does not alone make the rule content- or viewpoint-discriminatory, absent discrimination by subject matter or viewpoint in the sense of favoring one speaker’s perspective in ordinary public discourse.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Colorado is not invoking any historic and traditional category of unprotected speech (like obscenity, defamation, or true threats); it is instead disciplining a counselor for what she says in talk therapy based on the content and viewpoint of that counseling, which triggers heightened—indeed strict—scrutiny under our First Amendment architecture. NIFLA forecloses the State’s attempt to create a freestanding “professional speech” carve-out: that the counseling occurs in a licensed professional setting does not itself reduce First Amendment protection, and here the restriction targets the communicative message rather than merely regulating nonexpressive conduct that incidentally involves speech. Even accepting a compelling interest in protecting minors’ health and welfare, the State has not shown narrow tailoring in Ashcroft terms—i.e., that less speech-restrictive alternatives (informed-consent requirements, regulation of coercive practices, malpractice-style standards, or individualized discipline for demonstrable harm) “will not be as effective” as a categorical ban on one side of a contested therapeutic conversation. Because the law censors particular therapeutic goals and discussions rather than policing concrete misconduct, it chills protected speech and cannot survive the required scrutiny.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The activity Colorado seeks to regulate is talk therapy—communication between counselor and client—and on this record it is not the sale of an “ordinary commercial product” with merely incidental speech burdens but speech itself, delivered in the counselor’s own words to convey ideas and advice. Colorado’s law then turns on the content and viewpoint of that speech: it permits counseling that affirms certain outcomes about sexual orientation or gender identity while threatening professional discipline when the counselor engages in a disfavored direction of counseling aimed at different outcomes, effectively excising certain ideas from that dialogue. That is the kind of censorship the First Amendment does not tolerate, and the State may not evade heightened scrutiny by relabeling disfavored speech as “professional conduct.” Whatever the State’s asserted health interests, it must pursue them through means consistent with the Constitution, not by banning a viewpoint in the counseling room on pain of sanctions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado’s law, as applied to talk therapy between a licensed counselor and a client, regulates speech based on its content and, in practical operation, its viewpoint—allowing counseling that affirms certain sexual-orientation or gender-identity outcomes while forbidding counseling that aims at the opposite outcome. Under this Court’s precedents and the Nation’s history and tradition, States may regulate professional conduct and enforce generally applicable standards of care, but they may not evade the First Amendment by relabeling disfavored speech in the counseling room as “professional conduct,” especially where the restriction targets the communicative content of the treatment itself. NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” carve-out and directs heightened scrutiny for content-based regulations of speech by licensed professionals outside narrow, historically rooted exceptions (such as compelled factual disclosures in commercial/professional contexts). Given the law’s viewpoint-discriminatory structure and the serious chilling effect on counselor-client dialogue, the restriction is not practically workable under the First Amendment absent a far tighter fit than Colorado has shown.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The starting point is categorical First Amendment analysis: the State is not targeting speech as such, but regulating a treatment modality within a licensed profession—professional conduct—that is delivered through words, which fits within NIFLA’s recognition that regulation of conduct may incidentally involve speech without triggering a new, heightened constitutional “floor.” Colorado’s rule functions like a standard-of-care restriction on what a licensed counselor may do in treatment (aimed at changing a minor’s sexual orientation or gender identity), and the First Amendment has not historically required an added subjective-intent or viewpoint-exception requirement before States may discipline professionals for harmful or disallowed practices. Whatever additional safeguards one might prefer as a policy matter, legislatures’ choices about how to define or cabin permissible therapy do not themselves establish the constitutional baseline. Because this is a regulation of professional practice rather than a freestanding suppression of public debate, Colorado may enforce it consistent with the First Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The threshold question is the mechanism of the burden: Colorado is not merely setting background conditions of licensure while leaving speech untouched; it is disciplining a counselor based on the content (and, in operation, the direction) of what she says in the counseling room, so the case is properly analyzed as a direct speech restriction rather than as regulation of nonexpressive conduct that only incidentally involves speech. Under NIFLA, the State cannot invoke a broad “professional speech” carve-out, and this ban fits neither of NIFLA’s narrow categories (factual, noncontroversial disclosures; or regulation of a distinct medical procedure with only incidental speech), because the regulated “treatment” here is talk therapy itself. That content- and viewpoint-based targeting raises heightened scrutiny concerns and also risks chilling protected discussions between counselor and client by creating uncertainty about what therapeutic dialogue is permitted. On this record, Colorado has not shown that disciplining a counselor for particular therapeutic conversations can be sustained under the First Amendment framework that governs direct restrictions on speech.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may, consistent with the First Amendment, discipline a licensed mental-health counselor for engaging in certain talk-therapy communications with a client—treating those communications as regulable professional conduct rather than protected speech.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause), applied to Colorado’s restriction on licensed mental-health professionals’ provision of so-called “conversion therapy” (i.e., a state professional-licensing regulation that restricts what licensed counselors may say in counseling sessions, especially as to helping clients reduce same-sex attraction or change gender identity/expression).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Colorado law targets and censors viewpoints and content in the counseling room by forbidding particular messages and therapeutic conversations (while allowing the opposite perspective), and that because talk therapy is speech, the restriction should trigger heightened (at least strict) First Amendment scrutiny. She contends the State cannot re-label speech as ‘professional conduct’ merely because it occurs within a licensed relationship, and that the law suppresses counselors’ and clients’ ability to discuss and pursue goals rooted in personal, moral, or religious convictions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the statute is a permissible regulation of the practice of a licensed profession—i.e., professional conduct—aimed at protecting clients from harmful practices, especially minors, and that any burden on speech is incidental to regulating treatment. They maintain that the law does not exist to suppress ideas but to prevent a discredited and potentially harmful therapeutic intervention, and that states have broad authority to set standards of care and discipline professionals without triggering strict scrutiny whenever communications occur as part of treatment.
key_precedents: National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA) (2018)
Pickup v. Brown (9th Cir. 2014) (conversion-therapy regulation treated as conduct) (noted as part of the broader doctrinal landscape)
King v. Governor of New Jersey (3d Cir. 2014) (conversion-therapy restriction upheld under intermediate scrutiny) (noted as part of the broader doctrinal landscape)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest case that this is regulation of professional conduct—setting a standard of care for a defined intervention in a fiduciary relationship—and that any speech burden is incidental under NIFLA. But the threshold burden inquiry cannot be skipped: the statute’s trigger and enforcement mechanics turn on what is said in session and the therapeutic end the speech is intended to achieve, allowing “affirming” counseling while prohibiting change-oriented counseling, which is content- and viewpoint-based in operation as Justice Kavanaugh underscores. Even accepting the State’s interest in protecting minors, we must frame that interest at the level of this specific denial of an exemption—categorically banning one viewpoint in talk therapy—and the State has not shown why that step is necessary rather than pursuing viewpoint-neutral tools (discipline for coercion, deception, incompetence; informed consent). A narrowing construction of the kind Justice Kagan proposes only highlights that, as written, the law sweeps based on disfavored therapeutic messages and thus cannot be sustained on this record under heightened scrutiny.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor offer the State’s strongest point: that it is merely setting a standard of care for a defined treatment within a fiduciary, licensed relationship, and any speech burden is incidental. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, a common-sense Reed inquiry shows the statute’s trigger is the content and therapeutic aim of the counselor’s words—allowing “affirming” counseling while forbidding change-oriented counseling—which is viewpoint discrimination, not a neutral malpractice rule. NIFLA rejected carving out “professional speech” as a lesser-protected category, and relabeling a talk-therapy conversation as “conduct” does not solve the First Amendment problem when the supposed misconduct is the message itself. Even crediting contested legislative judgments about harm, Colorado has not shown narrow tailoring where viewpoint-neutral tools (fraud, coercion, informed consent, and ordinary malpractice standards) remain available.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is doctrinal fit: Colorado is said to be regulating a therapeutic “intervention” within a fiduciary, licensed relationship, with only incidental effects on speech. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, the statute’s operative trigger is not negligent or coercive conduct; it turns on the content and aim of the counselor’s words—allowing “affirming” counseling while forbidding counseling oriented toward “change”—which is textbook viewpoint discrimination under Reed and cannot be cured by relabeling talk therapy as “conduct” (NIFLA). Even accepting the State’s interest in protecting minors, the categorical, viewpoint-based ban is not shown to be necessary when Colorado can police coercion, deception, and incompetence through viewpoint-neutral malpractice and disciplinary standards. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrowing construction underscores the constitutional defect: if we must substantially cabin the law to avoid chilling ordinary counseling dialogue, that indicates the statute as written is aimed at suppressing disfavored ideas rather than regulating professional negligence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s central point—that the statute’s line can be described as permitting “affirming” counseling while forbidding “change-oriented” counseling—deserves to be confronted head-on, because that is how the law is framed in speech terms. But that framing still mistakes the operative trigger: Colorado is not licensing ideas in the public square; it is proscribing a defined treatment modality for minors within a fiduciary, State-created clinical relationship, and any burden on what is said is incidental to regulating the provision of that intervention as treatment. NIFLA rejects a freestanding “professional speech” carveout, yet it expressly preserves the State’s power to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and this case fits that lane better than a Reed-style censorship analysis. I agree with Justice Kagan that a cabined construction tethered to delivery of the intervention as treatment (not open-ended discussion, exploration, or referrals) supplies the limiting principle and avoids converting the First Amendment into a broad exemption from generally applicable licensure standards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh put the case at its highest pitch by describing the statute as permitting “affirming” counseling while forbidding “change-oriented” counseling—an account that would trigger Reed/NIFLA concerns about content and viewpoint discrimination. But that framing, as Justice Sotomayor underscores, skips the threshold doctrinal fit: Colorado is regulating a defined therapeutic intervention delivered in a licensed, fiduciary treatment relationship, where the State has long been allowed to set standards of care even when the treatment is administered through words. The First Amendment danger here is chilling ordinary therapeutic dialogue; the constitutional buffer is a narrowing construction tethering discipline to providing the proscribed intervention as treatment (not exploration, discussion, or referral), which keeps the rule in the lane NIFLA preserved—regulation of professional conduct with incidental speech effects. On that understanding, the State has limited no more speech than necessary to prevent a practice it has reasonably deemed harmful to minors.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson offer the State’s strongest point: Colorado is regulating a defined therapeutic intervention within a fiduciary, licensed relationship, and any effect on speech is merely incidental, especially if we adopt a narrowing construction cabining enforcement to the delivery of that “treatment.” But that reframing cannot change what the law makes dispositive—whether the counselor’s words are aimed at “affirming” or at “change”—so the State is defining forbidden “conduct” by disfavoring a particular viewpoint expressed in talk therapy. As the Chief Justice notes, calling the communication “conduct” does not avoid NIFLA’s insistence that we do not discount First Amendment protection merely because the speaker is a professional; and Justice Kavanaugh is right that the need to substantially narrow the statute to save it is evidence of its speech-directed operation. Colorado may pursue its interests through viewpoint-neutral tools (e.g., rules against coercion, deception, or malpractice), but it may not excise one side of a contested therapeutic viewpoint on pain of discipline.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that Colorado is regulating a therapeutic intervention within a licensed, fiduciary relationship and that NIFLA preserves state authority to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, this statute’s trigger still turns on the communicative content and therapeutic aim of what is said—allowing “affirming” counseling while forbidding change-oriented counseling—which is content- and viewpoint-based under a common-sense Reed/NIFLA inquiry, not a neutral standard-of-care rule keyed to coercion, fraud, or incompetence. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrowing construction underscores the First Amendment problem: if we must substantially rewrite the statute to confine it to “treatment” rather than ordinary dialogue, that confirms the law as written targets speech content and chills protected counseling. Even assuming a compelling interest in protecting minors, Colorado has not shown narrow tailoring when viewpoint-neutral tools (informed consent, malpractice, discipline for coercion/deception) are available on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the State’s best point: States may regulate professional conduct and standards of care in a fiduciary, licensed relationship, even when that conduct is carried out through words. But here the statute defines the proscribed “conduct” by the communicative content and therapeutic aim of what is said—allowing affirming counseling while forbidding change-oriented counseling—which, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, is classic viewpoint discrimination rather than a neutral malpractice rule keyed to coercion, deception, or incompetence. NIFLA cautions against recognizing a discounted “professional speech” lane, and I do not see a historically rooted, less-protected speech category that would lower the First Amendment baseline for private therapeutic dialogue. Justice Kagan’s proposed narrowing construction underscores that the law as written sweeps too broadly and would require judicial retooling to avoid chilling ordinary counseling discussions, which is a sign the statute cannot survive heightened scrutiny on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh make the most serious point: the statute can be described in content/viewpoint terms (affirming permitted; change-oriented forbidden). But that description prematurely selects a Reed/NIFLA speech-code frame rather than asking the threshold fit question—who is being regulated to do what, and why—when the State is disciplining licensed practitioners for administering a defined therapeutic intervention to minors within a fiduciary clinical relationship. Unlike Bantam Books-style censorship or a public-square orthodoxy rule, this operates through licensure standards governing treatment, and NIFLA itself preserves the State’s authority to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech. Justice Kagan’s cabining principle remains critical: if construed and applied as targeting the provision of the intervention as treatment (not open-ended exploration, discussion, or referral), the speech burden is sufficiently integrated and non-attenuated to fall on the conduct-regulation side of the line rather than triggering strict scrutiny by default.

John Roberts.reasoning: The threshold question is whether Colorado’s action burdens protected speech, and here it does: the State proposes to discipline a counselor for words spoken in a counseling session based on what those words communicate—permitting counseling that affirms same-sex attraction or gender transition goals while forbidding counseling aimed at reducing same-sex attraction or changing gender identity/expression, which the speaker and listener reasonably understand as a content- and viewpoint-based restriction. Colorado cannot avoid that burden by relabeling talk therapy as mere “conduct,” because the regulated act is the communication itself rather than some independently regulable procedure, and our cases reject a free-floating “professional speech” carveout that would dilute ordinary First Amendment scrutiny. Once the law is correctly characterized as a content-based restriction on speech, Colorado must justify this particular application with a tightly framed interest and a fit showing why disciplining this counselor for these communications is necessary rather than relying on broadly formulated appeals to regulating the profession generally. On this record, the State’s asserted interests in protecting clients and maintaining standards of care are too generalized to sustain a viewpoint-discriminatory speech ban as applied to counseling conversations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado’s law, as applied to talk therapy, regulates speech “because of its message” by forbidding counseling communications that pursue one set of outcomes (reducing same-sex attraction or changing gender identity/expression) while permitting the opposite perspective—making it content based under a common-sense Reed inquiry and therefore presumptively invalid. The State cannot evade that conclusion by relabeling the counseling conversation as “professional conduct,” because the regulated activity is the counselor’s words to the client, not an independent nonexpressive act. Because the restriction is content based, Colorado bears the burden under strict scrutiny to show a compelling interest pursued through narrow tailoring, and it has not done so where the law censors particular viewpoints in the counseling room rather than targeting demonstrably harmful conduct by less speech-restrictive means. Nor should judge-made doctrines or deference to asserted expert consensus dilute the First Amendment’s baseline rule against content discrimination where the statute’s operative trigger is the content of what the counselor says.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado’s law regulates what a licensed counselor may say to a client in a counseling session based on the content and viewpoint of the message—permitting affirming discussions while forbidding communications aimed at reducing same-sex attraction or changing gender identity/expression. Under a textual and practical reading of the First Amendment, the State cannot evade heightened scrutiny by relabeling core communicative activity as “professional conduct” simply because it occurs within a licensed relationship; talk therapy is speech, not a physical procedure with merely incidental speech effects. While States have substantial authority to police malpractice and require informed consent, a categorical ban on disfavored counseling viewpoints is different in kind and risks converting licensing boards into censors. Because the restriction is content- and viewpoint-based and not tied to a generally applicable standard of professional negligence, it must satisfy at least strict scrutiny, which Colorado has not met on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado is regulating the practice of a licensed profession—treatment provided to clients in a fiduciary, state-created licensing relationship—rather than targeting public expression, and any burden on what a counselor may say occurs incidentally to the State’s regulation of professional conduct and standards of care. The operative trigger is the provision of counseling services to clients (particularly minors) under a state license, not the counselor’s viewpoint in the abstract; the State may discipline a practitioner for employing a discredited and harmful therapeutic intervention even if that intervention is delivered through words. This case does not require creating a broad First Amendment “exemption” from generally applicable professional-licensing rules simply because the regulated treatment is talk therapy. Consistent with NIFLA, the State remains free to prohibit substandard or harmful professional conduct (including conduct carried out through speech) without thereby “dictat[ing] the content of speech” in the way compelled-speech doctrine addresses.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The threshold question is how to classify what Colorado has regulated: here the State has not criminalized the counselor’s viewpoints in public debate, but has set a professional standard of care for licensed mental-health treatment of minors, delivered in the context of a fiduciary, state-licensed therapeutic relationship. Under that framing, the regulation targets professional conduct—providing a particular form of treatment—though that conduct is carried out through words, and the First Amendment problem is whether the State has swept so broadly that it will chill protected counseling conversations (including open-ended exploration) rather than just proscribe a defined therapeutic intervention. Colorado may discipline a licensee for engaging in a practice the State has reasonably deemed harmful to minors, so long as the line is cabined to the provision of that intervention (not mere discussion, information, or exploration), thereby limiting no more speech than necessary to protect patients and avoid deterring lawful therapeutic dialogue. Because the law operates within licensure and treatment and can be construed to leave room for non-directive counseling and discussion, I would uphold it as a permissible regulation of professional conduct that only incidentally burdens speech.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The threshold question is whether Colorado is regulating ordinary professional conduct with only incidental effects on speech, or instead directly regulating “pure speech”; talk therapy consists of words chosen to convey ideas, and the statute turns entirely on what a counselor may say to a client about sexual orientation or gender identity. By forbidding counseling that seeks to reduce same-sex attraction or change gender identity while permitting counseling that affirms or encourages the opposite, the State is engaging in content- and viewpoint-based regulation that functions to excise certain ideas from the counseling room on pain of professional discipline. Under compelled-speech and anti-censorship principles (Barnette, Hurley, Dale), the State may not leverage a licensing regime to force speakers to adhere to the government’s preferred orthodoxy or to silence disfavored viewpoints, even if it invokes a protective purpose. NIFLA confirms there is no freestanding “professional speech” exception allowing heightened control over disfavored messages; when the law targets the content of what professionals say rather than neutrally policing malpractice through generally applicable standards, strict scrutiny is triggered and is not satisfied here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction is content- and viewpoint-based because it turns on “whether the counselor is speaking about a particular topic” (efforts to reduce same-sex attraction or change gender identity/expression) and, in practical operation, permits counseling that affirms those traits while forbidding counseling aimed at change. Under NIFLA, the State may not relabel speech as “professional conduct” simply because it occurs within a licensed counseling relationship; talk therapy is speech, and this is not a regulation of nonexpressive conduct that only incidentally burdens speech. Because heightened scrutiny is triggered, the State must show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring/least restrictive means, and broad censorship of a disfavored therapeutic viewpoint is not the least restrictive way to protect clients (including minors) given the availability of informed-consent, disclosure, and disciplinary rules targeting coercion, fraud, or malpractice irrespective of viewpoint. The First Amendment therefore bars disciplining the counselor based on the content of her counseling communications.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The law disciplines a counselor for the content of in-session talk therapy—i.e., for saying certain things (and pursuing certain client-directed goals) while allowing the opposite messages—so the State is not merely regulating nonexpressive conduct but imposing a content- and viewpoint-based speech restriction. Under a categorical First Amendment approach, the State has not shown that this counseling speech fits within any historically recognized unprotected category (like threats, fraud, or obscenity), so it remains presumptively protected. NIFLA forecloses treating “professional speech” as a lesser-protected category, and although States may regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, Colorado’s rule targets speech itself as the mechanism of the prohibited treatment. Because the restriction operates by censoring particular therapeutic messages rather than by enforcing an objective, generally applicable standard of care divorced from viewpoint, it triggers heightened scrutiny that Colorado has not satisfied on these facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The threshold task is selecting the right First Amendment framework for these facts: Colorado is not pressuring third-party distributors or platforms to suppress speech (so Bantam Books–style coercion does not fit), and the discipline turns on what a licensed counselor does within a fiduciary treatment relationship, so the more apt inquiry is whether the State is regulating professional conduct that incidentally involves speech. Here, the challenged law targets a defined therapeutic intervention when delivered as treatment to clients (especially minors), and its speech impact is direct but integrated into the provision of care rather than functioning like a general public speech ban; that fit places it within NIFLA’s acknowledgement that States may regulate professional conduct even when it is carried out through words. Applying that framework, Colorado’s asserted interest in protecting clients from harmful or substandard treatment and enforcing standards of care can justify the restriction so long as it is cabined to treatment contexts and does not sweep more broadly into abstract advocacy or generalized counseling advice outside the clinical setting. On this record, the regulation’s operation as a licensing/standard-of-care measure—rather than a public-facing viewpoint-suppression regime—supports upholding it.
